title: THE DISEASE WAS IN HIS FEET—BUT THE DEEPER SICKNESS WAS SOMEWHERE ELSE
paragraphs: THE DISEASE WAS IN HIS FEET—BUT THE DEEPER SICKNESS WAS SOMEWHERE ELSE

King Asa once cried to God when an army overwhelmed him. Years later, when disease overwhelmed his own body, Scripture records one devastating sentence: he sought the physicians—but did not seek the LORD. What happened between those two moments may be one of the most frightening warnings ever written for people who have walked with God for years.
There are Bible verses that comfort you.
There are Bible verses that strengthen you.
And then there are verses that seem to quietly follow you out of the room.
Second Chronicles 16:12 is one of them.
“In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa became diseased in his feet, and his malady was severe; yet in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but the physicians.”
Read that slowly.
Because the tragedy is not simply that a king became sick.
The tragedy is that a man who once knew where to run...
apparently forgot.
And perhaps that is why Asa's story can become painfully personal.
Because some of us have not stopped believing in God.
We have simply stopped seeking Him first.
We know Christian language. We know worship songs. We know what verses to post when someone else is hurting. We know how to say, “God is faithful.”
But when our own world begins collapsing, something else reveals what we actually trust.
The bank account.
The specialist.
The relationship.
The influential friend.
The strategy.
The medication.
The career.
Our own intelligence.
None of those things is necessarily sinful.
That distinction matters enormously.

Second Chronicles 16:12 should not be twisted into an argument that Christians should reject physicians, medicine, or legitimate medical treatment. Scripture itself does not say that Asa sinned merely because physicians were involved. The accusation is much more precise—and far more uncomfortable:
“he did not seek the LORD.”
That is the wound beneath the wound.
The Hebrew text makes the contrast striking:
וְגַם־בָּחֳלְיוֹ לֹא־דָרַשׁ אֶת־יְהוָה כִּי בָּרֹפְאִים
vegam-baḥolyō lo-darash et-YHWH, ki barofe'im
The crucial expression is לֹא־דָרַשׁ אֶת־יְהוָה — lo-darash et-YHWH:
“He did not seek the LORD.”
The verb darash carries the sense of seeking, inquiring, resorting to, turning toward.
And that word matters because Asa's story is fundamentally a story about where a human heart turns when pressure comes.
Not merely where his feet hurt.
Where his heart turned.
That makes the story frightening because Asa was not some lifelong pagan king who had never experienced God's faithfulness.
He knew better.
Long before diseased feet confined him, Asa had stood before something far more terrifying.
An enormous enemy force came against Judah.
And the younger Asa did something beautiful.
He prayed.
“O LORD, there is none beside thee to help, between the mighty and him that hath no strength: help us, O LORD our God; for we rely on thee...” — 2 Chronicles 14:11
There it is.
The heartbeat of the younger Asa:
“We rely on You.”
He looked at an enemy he could not defeat and essentially said,
God, if You do not help us, we are finished.
And God delivered them.
Asa had lived the testimony people dream about having.
He had watched helplessness become the stage upon which God's power was displayed.
Later, Azariah came with another message:
“The LORD is with you, while ye be with him; and if ye seek him, he will be found of you...” — 2 Chronicles 15:2
There is our word again.
Seek.
Asa responded.
He removed idols.
He repaired the altar.
He gathered the people.
They entered covenant together to seek the LORD.
There was rejoicing.
There was reform.
There was rest.
There was evidence everywhere that God had been faithful.
And that is precisely what makes the ending hurt.
Because years passed.
Success accumulated.
Experience accumulated.
Power accumulated.
And somewhere along the road, the man who once knew how desperately he needed God began behaving as though he could manage without Him.
Maybe you know that road.
Not rebellion with flashing lights.
Not waking up one morning and declaring that Jesus is no longer Lord.
Something quieter.
You used to pray before making decisions.
Now you make them and ask God to bless them afterward.
You used to open Scripture because you were hungry.
Now you mostly encounter verses while scrolling.
You used to confess quickly.
Now you explain yourself.
You used to tremble at conviction.
Now conviction irritates you.
You used to say, “Lord, what do You want?”
Now the first question is, “What do I want?”
Nothing dramatic happened.
You just slowly learned how to live while depending less consciously upon God.
Then came Ramah.
Baasha king of Israel threatened Judah.
And Asa faced another crisis.
Years earlier, an overwhelming army had made Asa pray.
This time, Asa calculated.
He took silver and gold from the treasuries of the house of the LORD and sent them to Ben-hadad, king of Syria, seeking an alliance.
Strategically?
It worked.
Baasha withdrew.
The immediate problem disappeared.
And this may be one of the most dangerous moments in the entire story.
Because sometimes something can work and still reveal that your heart is moving away from God.
Success is not always proof that our spiritual condition is healthy.
Hanani the seer confronted Asa:
“Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God...” — 2 Chronicles 16:7
There it is again.
Reliance.
The issue that had once been Asa's strength was becoming his downfall.
Then Hanani reminded him of the past.
God had delivered Asa before.
God had already proved Himself.
And then came one of Scripture's magnificent declarations:
“For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him...” — 2 Chronicles 16:9
God was not reluctant to help Asa.
Think about that.
The Lord was looking to show Himself strong.
Asa's tragedy was not that God's arm had suddenly become too short.
Asa had changed where he placed his confidence.
And when confronted...
he did not repent.
He became angry.
He imprisoned the messenger.
He oppressed people.
This is where the story becomes almost unbearable.
The young Asa cried to God because he knew he was weak.
The older Asa became furious when someone reminded him that he was weak.
Have you ever wondered whether this is happening to you?
There was a time when correction brought you to your knees.
Now correction makes you defensive.
There was a time when Scripture exposed something and you whispered,
“Lord... change me.”
Now your instinct is,
“That doesn't apply to me.”
That is dangerous ground.
Because one of the most frightening spiritual conditions is not weakness.
It is becoming unable to admit weakness.
Then three years after the confrontation with Hanani, Scripture tells us about Asa's feet.
His disease became severe.
The Bible does not give us enough information to diagnose the precise illness, and responsible interpretation should resist pretending otherwise.
We know what Scripture wants us to know.
It was serious.
It affected his feet.
And in the midst of it, Asa still did not seek the LORD.
Do you see the tragedy now?
The feet are almost the final scene of a much longer spiritual story.
Asa had already stopped relying upon God during national crisis.
He had already rejected prophetic correction.
He had already hardened himself.
The physical disease did not create the deeper problem.
It exposed it.
And this is where we must be careful.
The lesson is not:
“Never go to a doctor.”
Please do not turn this passage into something Scripture itself does not say.
God can work through physicians.
God can work through medicine.
God can work through surgery, therapy, treatment, wise counselors, skilled professionals, friends, employers, and ordinary human means.
The issue is not whether you use means.
The question is whether the means have replaced the God upon whom your soul ultimately depends.
You can pray on the way to the hospital.
You can seek the LORD while receiving chemotherapy.
You can trust God while taking prescribed medicine.
You can ask God for wisdom while sitting across from a physician.
Faith and appropriate medical care do not have to be enemies.
The problem begins when created help becomes our functional god.
When we seek everybody...
except Him.
When we Google before we pray.
Panic before we pray.
Call everyone before we pray.
Strategize before we pray.
Spend before we pray.
Post before we pray.
And sometimes we do eventually pray...
after every other door has failed.
As though Jesus were the emergency exit instead of Lord.
Maybe your “physicians” are not physicians at all.
Maybe yours is a person you cannot imagine living without.
Maybe it is money.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe alcohol.
Maybe constant entertainment because silence forces you to confront what is happening inside you.
Maybe it is approval.
Maybe you need people to tell you that you matter because somewhere along the way you stopped resting in what Christ says about you.
Maybe you have become extraordinarily skilled at managing symptoms while refusing to bring the disease of your heart into the light.
And perhaps nobody knows.
You still smile.
Still attend church.
Still share Bible verses.
Still tell everyone God is good.
But privately?
You are exhausted.
Something hurts.
Something has been hurting for a long time.
And instead of running toward Jesus, you have become very good at surviving around the pain.
Please hear the Gospel here.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to teach damaged people better coping strategies.
He came to save sinners.
He came for people whose deepest disease could never be cured by human effort.
Sin has gone deeper than our habits.
Deeper than our image.
Deeper than the things other people can see.
And we cannot heal ourselves.
That is why the Gospel is not “try harder.”
The Gospel is Christ.
The eternal Son of God took on flesh.
He lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He carried sin to the cross.
He suffered under judgment.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And He rose again.
The scandal of Christianity is not that good people can improve enough for God to accept them.
It is that guilty people can be forgiven because Jesus Christ took the place of sinners.
Grace does not pretend your sin is small.
Grace says the cross was sufficient.
And this is where Asa's story reaches through centuries and puts a hand on our shoulder.
You may have drifted.
You may have trusted other things.
You may have resisted correction.
You may have wasted years.
You may have known God faithfully in another season and barely recognize your heart now.
But while you are breathing, the invitation of the Gospel is still:
Come.
Not after you fix yourself.
Come now.
Repentance means you stop defending what God is exposing.
You turn.
You confess.
You come back to Christ.
And 1 John 1:9 gives sinners extraordinary hope: if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Maybe your prayer does not need impressive language tonight.
Maybe it simply needs honesty.
Jesus...
I have been seeking everything except You.
Forgive me.
I have trusted things You created more than I trusted You.
Forgive me.
I have become defensive when You tried to correct me.
Forgive me.
I have learned how to look spiritually alive while becoming dry inside.
Forgive me.
I need You.
Not merely Your blessings.
Not merely Your rescue.
Not merely Your healing.
You.
And maybe that is the sentence somebody reading this has been avoiding for years.
“I need You.”
There is no shame in needing Christ.
That is Christianity.
The strongest believer in the room is still breathing borrowed breath.
The mature Christian has not graduated from dependence upon Jesus.
We never outgrow grace.
We never become too experienced for prayer.
We never become too knowledgeable for Scripture.
We never become too successful to kneel.
And we never become so spiritually mature that Jesus becomes optional.
Asa's beginning warns us not to trust ourselves.
Asa's ending warns us not to assume yesterday's faithfulness guarantees today's dependence.
But the Gospel directs our eyes beyond Asa.
To a better King.
Asa faltered.
Jesus did not.
Asa's heart wandered.
Christ remained perfectly obedient to the Father.
Asa could not save himself.
Jesus saves completely those who come to God through Him.
That is why our hope is ultimately not that we will become strong enough never to stumble.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
The King who does not fail.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The Shepherd who searches for wandering sheep.
The Advocate for those who confess.
The Redeemer who can take chapters we are ashamed of and make them evidence of His mercy.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
There may come a day when the diagnosis arrives, the relationship breaks, the money disappears, the plan fails, or fear starts whispering at 2:00 in the morning.
On that day, remember Asa.
Then remember Jesus.

Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not. We are saved by grace, not by social-media activity—but because sharing biblical truth can place the Gospel in front of someone you may never know is struggling. Our glory belongs to God alone; our support of Gospel work should flow from gratitude to Him, never from an attempt to purchase His approval.
But whatever you do after reading this, never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting the Savior.
You need Jesus.
No purchase can save you.
No share can cleanse you.
No comment can reconcile you to God.
No ministry membership can substitute for repentance and faith.
Only Christ saves.
So seek the doctor when you need the doctor.
Take wise counsel when you need wise counsel.
Receive legitimate help without shame.
But underneath every appointment, every treatment, every strategy, every relationship, every resource, every unanswered question and every frightening night...
seek the LORD.
Because the saddest sentence in Asa's story was not that his feet became diseased.
It was that when suffering came, the man who once knew how to seek God no longer sought Him.
Do not let that become the final sentence of your story.
Your deepest tragedy would not be discovering that your feet could no longer carry you—it would be forgetting the Savior who carried you all along.
